name: Lunar New Year
visual_anchor: A happy family in bright red clothes hanging red paper lanterns and gold decorations outside their home, a cheerful lion dancer in the street behind them, warm festive glow, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A big celebration that usually falls in late January or February
Homes fill with red decorations, dumplings and family reunions
Each year is linked to one of twelve zodiac animals
In China it is also called the Spring Festival

facts_and_myths.claim: Each Lunar New Year is matched with one of 12 zodiac animals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Chinese zodiac cycles through 12 animals, from the Rat to the Pig, one for each year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many families clean their homes before the new year to sweep away last year's bad luck.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lunar New Year falls on the same calendar date every year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It follows the Moon, so the date moves around between late January and mid-February.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The holiday travel rush in China is often called the largest yearly human migration on Earth.

name: Tet
visual_anchor: A smiling Vietnamese family gathered beside a blooming pink peach blossom branch and a little kumquat tree full of orange fruit, square green rice cakes on the table, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: The biggest and most important holiday of the year in Vietnam
Children receive lucky money in little red envelopes
Families wrap square sticky rice cakes in green leaves
Peach blossoms decorate homes in the north and yellow apricot blossoms in the south

facts_and_myths.claim: Families make square sticky rice cakes called banh chung for Tet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Banh chung is filled with mung beans and pork, then wrapped in leaves and boiled for hours.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditionally, many Vietnamese people counted themselves one year older at Tet instead of on birthdays.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tet is celebrated in just one single day.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tet celebrations last several days, with the biggest family visits during the first three days.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Little kumquat trees covered in orange fruit are a popular Tet decoration for good luck.

name: Mid-Autumn Festival
visual_anchor: Children carrying glowing star-shaped and rabbit-shaped lanterns under a huge golden full moon, a plate of mooncakes on a garden table nearby, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: An autumn celebration held on a bright full moon night
Families share round pastries and admire the Moon together
Children parade with glowing lanterns, often shaped like stars or rabbits
Held on the 15th day of the 8th month of the lunar calendar

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mid-Autumn Festival takes place on a full moon night.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It falls on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, when the Moon is full and bright.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Vietnam, Mid-Autumn is especially a children's festival, with lion dances and star lanterns.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mid-Autumn Festival is always on the same September date.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It follows the lunar calendar, so it moves between mid-September and early October.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A famous legend tells of Chang'e, a lady who lives on the Moon with a jade rabbit.

name: Lantern Festival
visual_anchor: A night street hung with hundreds of glowing red and gold lanterns, children pointing up at a lantern shaped like a fish, bowls of round sweet rice balls on a stall, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A night festival filled with glowing lanterns of every shape
People try to solve riddles written on lanterns
Families eat sweet round rice balls in warm soup
Marks the end of the Lunar New Year season on the first full moon

facts_and_myths.claim: People solve riddles written on lanterns during the Lantern Festival.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Guessing lantern riddles is a classic tradition, and good guessers sometimes win small prizes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sweet sticky rice balls called tangyuan are the favorite treat of the Lantern Festival.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Lantern Festival happens on the first day of Lunar New Year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It is held on the 15th day of the first lunar month, closing the New Year celebrations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It falls on the very first full moon of the lunar year.

name: Diwali
visual_anchor: A doorway glowing with rows of small clay oil lamps, a bright flower-shaped rangoli pattern in pink, orange and yellow on the floor, a smiling child holding a plate of sweets, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A joyful autumn celebration full of lights, sweets and new clothes
Families light rows of small clay lamps around their homes
Colorful patterns are drawn at doorways to welcome guests
Widely celebrated in India, usually in October or November

facts_and_myths.claim: Diwali is often called the Festival of Lights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Homes, streets and shops sparkle with lamps, candles and string lights during the celebration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The small clay oil lamps lit for Diwali are called diyas.

facts_and_myths.claim: Diwali is celebrated for only one evening.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Diwali celebrations usually stretch over five days, with the main night in the middle.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Families often swap boxes of sweets with neighbors and friends during Diwali.

name: Holi
visual_anchor: Laughing children tossing clouds of pink, yellow, green and blue powder into the sunny spring air, their white clothes splashed with rainbow colors, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A cheerful spring celebration that gets everyone very messy
People toss bright colored powder and splash colored water
White clothes end up covered in every color of the rainbow
Held on a full moon, usually in March, in India and Nepal

facts_and_myths.claim: During Holi, people throw bright colored powder at each other.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Friends and family chase each other with colored powder and water to welcome spring.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many people wear white on purpose so the colors show up brightly.

facts_and_myths.claim: Holi is celebrated only in India.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Holi is also a major holiday in Nepal, and communities around the world join the fun.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Holi marks the arrival of spring and the end of winter.

name: Christmas
visual_anchor: A cozy living room with a sparkling decorated tree, wrapped presents with red bows underneath, stockings by the fireplace and snow falling outside the window, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A winter holiday famous for presents and family dinners
Homes are decorated with lights and evergreen trees
Kids hang stockings and wait for Santa Claus
Celebrated on December 25 in most countries

facts_and_myths.claim: Christmas is celebrated on December 25 in most countries.
facts_and_myths.explanation: December 25 is the main Christmas Day for most families around the world.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Australia, Christmas falls in summer, so many families enjoy beach picnics.

facts_and_myths.claim: A soda company invented Santa Claus's red suit.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Santa was drawn in red in many illustrations long before the famous 1930s soda ads.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The tradition of decorating Christmas trees at home is credited to Germany.

name: Halloween
visual_anchor: Smiling kids dressed as a friendly pumpkin, a superhero and a bumblebee holding candy buckets on a porch lined with cheerful carved pumpkins, orange autumn leaves all around, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A fun autumn night when kids dress up in costumes
Children go door to door saying "trick or treat" for candy
Carved pumpkins with glowing faces sit on porches
Celebrated every year on October 31

facts_and_myths.claim: Kids go trick-or-treating for candy on Halloween.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Children in costumes visit neighbors' doors and collect treats, ideally with an adult nearby.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pumpkins are actually fruits, because they grow from flowers and hold seeds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dressing up in costumes for Halloween started in the United States.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Costumed door-to-door visiting, called guising, came from Scotland and Ireland before spreading to America.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Halloween is celebrated on the same date every year: October 31.

name: Thanksgiving
visual_anchor: A big family smiling around a long dinner table with a golden roast turkey, mashed potatoes, corn and pumpkin pie, autumn leaves decorating the room, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: An autumn holiday about being grateful and sharing a big meal
Roast turkey and pumpkin pie are the classic foods
A parade with giant character balloons marches through New York City
In the United States it falls on the fourth Thursday of November

facts_and_myths.claim: US Thanksgiving is on the fourth Thursday of November.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The date changes each year, but it is always the fourth Thursday of November.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Each year the US president pardons a turkey, which then lives happily on a farm.

facts_and_myths.claim: Canada celebrates Thanksgiving on the same day as the United States.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Canadian Thanksgiving is earlier, on the second Monday of October.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Giant balloons in the New York parade can be taller than a five-story building.

name: Songkran
visual_anchor: Smiling children in colorful flower-print shirts splashing water from bowls and buckets on a sunny street in Thailand, sparkling droplets flying everywhere, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A giant splashy street party in hot weather
People soak each other with buckets and water sprayers
Younger people gently pour water over elders' hands to show respect
The traditional New Year of Thailand, held in mid-April

facts_and_myths.claim: During Songkran, people splash water on each other in the streets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water stands for washing away the old year and starting fresh and cool.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Songkran happens in mid-April, one of the hottest times of the year in Thailand.

facts_and_myths.claim: Songkran is a New Year party held on January 1.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Songkran is the traditional Thai New Year and is celebrated in mid-April.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gently pouring scented water over elders' hands is a way to show respect and ask for blessings.

name: Carnival of Rio de Janeiro
visual_anchor: A dazzling parade float shaped like a giant colorful parrot, dancers in sparkly feathered costumes in green, yellow and blue, bright stadium lights at night, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A huge, colorful street party full of music and dancing
Dancers wear sparkling costumes with giant feathers
Samba schools compete with enormous parade floats
Held each year in February or early March in a famous Brazilian city

facts_and_myths.claim: Samba schools parade in a special stadium called the Sambadrome.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Sambadrome is a long parade avenue with grandstands where samba schools perform and compete.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Samba schools spend almost a whole year building their floats and costumes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rio's Carnival takes place every year in December.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rio's Carnival is held in February or early March, and the exact dates change each year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Brazil is in the Southern Hemisphere, so Carnival happens during summer.

name: Hanami
visual_anchor: A family having a picnic on a blue blanket under blooming pink cherry trees in a Japanese park, soft petals drifting through the sunny air, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A springtime custom of enjoying pretty flowering trees
Friends and families picnic in parks under pink blossoms
News reports follow the blossoms as they bloom from south to north
Its name means 'flower viewing' in Japanese

facts_and_myths.claim: Hanami means 'flower viewing' in Japanese.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hana means flower and mi means looking, and today it mostly means admiring cherry blossoms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Japan has a cherry blossom forecast that tracks the blooms moving north across the country.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cherry blossoms stay on the trees for most of the summer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Full bloom lasts only about one to two weeks before the petals fall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Viewing cherry blossoms lit up at night has its own name: yozakura.

name: Dragon Boat Festival
visual_anchor: Long colorful boats with carved dragon heads racing across a sparkling river, teams paddling together while a drummer keeps the beat, cheering crowds on the shore, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: An early-summer festival full of exciting races on the water
Teams paddle long boats decorated with dragon heads and tails
People eat sticky rice parcels wrapped in bamboo leaves
Held on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month

facts_and_myths.claim: People eat zongzi, sticky rice wrapped in leaves, at this festival.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Zongzi are pyramid-shaped rice parcels with sweet or savory fillings, steamed or boiled in leaves.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A drummer sits at the front of each boat to keep all the paddlers in rhythm.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dragon boat racing only happens in China.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dragon boat racing is now an international sport, with teams in many countries around the world.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A steersperson stands at the back of the boat to steer it straight.

name: La Tomatina
visual_anchor: A cheerful crowd wearing goggles and white t-shirts splattered with red tomato pulp in a narrow sunny Spanish street, squishy tomatoes flying through the air, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A summer festival that turns into a giant food fight
Everyone throws squishy ripe tomatoes at each other
The streets turn red and get washed down afterward
Held on the last Wednesday of August in the Spanish town of Buñol

facts_and_myths.claim: At La Tomatina, people throw squashed tomatoes at each other for fun.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Trucks bring piles of overripe tomatoes, and everyone joins a big, messy tomato fight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Players must squash tomatoes before throwing them so nobody gets hurt.

facts_and_myths.claim: La Tomatina takes place in Italy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: La Tomatina is held in Buñol, a small town near Valencia in Spain.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fire trucks hose down the streets afterward to wash away the tomato mess.

name: Ao Dai
visual_anchor: A smiling young woman in a flowing pale blue silk tunic with long side panels over white trousers, holding a conical hat beside a lotus pond, soft morning light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: An elegant outfit with a long, flowing tunic
The tunic has high side slits and is worn over loose trousers
Many high school girls wear a white version as a uniform
The national traditional dress of Vietnam

facts_and_myths.claim: The ao dai is a long tunic worn over loose trousers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its long front and back panels flow freely thanks to slits up both sides.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Vietnam, many high school girls wear white ao dai as their school uniform.

facts_and_myths.claim: Only women ever wear the ao dai.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Men wear ao dai too, especially for weddings, Tet and other special occasions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name ao dai means 'long shirt' in Vietnamese.

name: Kimono
visual_anchor: A smiling girl in a bright red kimono with white crane patterns and a wide gold sash, standing on a wooden bridge in a Japanese garden, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A long robe with wide, flowing sleeves
It is shaped like the letter T when laid flat
A wide sash called an obi is tied around the waist
The traditional clothing of Japan

facts_and_myths.claim: A kimono is tied at the waist with a wide sash called an obi.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The obi holds the kimono closed and is often tied in a decorative knot at the back.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A light cotton summer kimono, popular at festivals, is called a yukata.

facts_and_myths.claim: Kimonos are only worn by women.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Men wear kimonos too, usually in darker colors with simpler patterns.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word kimono simply means 'thing to wear' in Japanese.

name: Hanbok
visual_anchor: A cheerful girl in a short pink jacket with rainbow-striped sleeves and a full, bell-shaped green skirt, standing in front of a colorful Korean palace gate, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A bright, colorful outfit worn on special holidays
Women wear a short jacket with a long, full skirt
Men wear a jacket with roomy trousers
The traditional clothing of Korea

facts_and_myths.claim: A woman's hanbok has a short jacket and a long, full skirt.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The short jacket is called a jeogori and the wide, flowing skirt is called a chima.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Visitors wearing hanbok can enter Seoul's royal palaces for free.

facts_and_myths.claim: The hanbok is the traditional clothing of Japan.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The hanbok comes from Korea; Japan's traditional robe is the kimono.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many Korean families wear hanbok for Lunar New Year and the autumn harvest festival Chuseok.

name: Sari
visual_anchor: A smiling woman in a shimmering orange and magenta draped garment with a golden border, one end flowing over her shoulder, standing in a sunny marigold garden, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A long, colorful garment that is wrapped instead of sewn
One end is draped gracefully over the shoulder
It is worn with a short fitted blouse
Commonly worn in India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka

facts_and_myths.claim: A sari is one long piece of cloth wrapped without any sewing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The unstitched cloth is pleated, wrapped around the waist and draped over the shoulder.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A sari is usually about five to nine yards long.

facts_and_myths.claim: Saris are worn only in India.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Saris are also widely worn in Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: There are dozens of different regional styles for draping a sari.

name: Kilt
visual_anchor: A smiling bagpiper in a red and green checkered knee-length pleated garment and knee socks, standing on a misty green Scottish hillside, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A knee-length pleated garment wrapped around the waist
Usually made from cloth with a crisscross checkered pattern
Often worn by bagpipers with a small pouch on the front
Traditional menswear of the Scottish Highlands

facts_and_myths.claim: Kilts are often made of tartan, a cloth with crisscross stripes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tartan is woven with colored stripes that cross each other to make a checkered pattern.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many Scottish family clans have their very own tartan pattern.

facts_and_myths.claim: Kilts are skirts made only for women.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The kilt is traditional clothing for men in Scotland, worn at weddings, parades and Highland games.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kilts have no pockets, so a pouch called a sporran is worn on the front.

name: Sombrero
visual_anchor: A smiling mariachi musician holding a guitar and wearing a huge round hat with an extra-wide brim and colorful embroidery, under a bright blue Mexican sky, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A hat with an extra-wide, round brim
Made to shade the head, neck and shoulders from strong sun
Mariachi musicians often wear fancy decorated versions
A famous traditional hat from Mexico

facts_and_myths.claim: The name sombrero comes from the Spanish word for shade.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sombra means shade in Spanish, and the wide brim keeps the wearer in shade.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A galaxy far away is named the Sombrero Galaxy because it looks like this hat.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sombreros were first invented as silly party costume hats.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They began as practical work hats for farmers and horse riders under the hot sun.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Mexican Hat Dance is a famous folk dance performed around a sombrero.

name: Poncho
visual_anchor: A smiling child in a striped red, orange and blue woolen cloak with a hole for the head, standing beside a fluffy white alpaca in the Andes mountains, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A cozy outer garment you pull on over your head
Basically a big piece of cloth with a hole in the middle
Traditional versions are woven from alpaca or llama wool
Comes from the Andes mountains of South America

facts_and_myths.claim: A poncho is a blanket-like cloth with a hole for the head.
facts_and_myths.explanation: You slip your head through the opening and the cloth hangs down to keep you warm.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditional Andean ponchos are often woven from soft alpaca or llama wool.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ponchos were first made as plastic rain gear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: People in South America wove woolen ponchos for warmth for centuries before plastic existed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gauchos, the cowboys of Argentina, wore ponchos while riding across the grassy plains.

name: Dirndl
visual_anchor: A smiling girl in a dress with a fitted green top, white puffy-sleeved blouse, full red skirt and blue apron, standing in a flowery Alpine meadow with snowy mountains behind, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A cheerful dress worn with a white blouse
It has a fitted top, a full skirt and an apron
Began as everyday work clothing in mountain villages
Traditional dress of Bavaria in Germany and of Austria

facts_and_myths.claim: A dirndl has a fitted top, a full skirt and an apron.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The dress is worn over a short white blouse, with a colorful apron tied on top.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The dirndl started as simple work clothing for women in the Alps.

facts_and_myths.claim: The dirndl comes from France.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The dirndl comes from the Alpine regions of Bavaria in Germany and of Austria.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the same region, men traditionally wear leather shorts called lederhosen.

name: Qipao
visual_anchor: A smiling woman in a fitted red silk dress with gold flower embroidery, a high standing collar and knotted cloth buttons, standing beside red paper lanterns, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A fitted, elegant one-piece dress often made of silk
It has a high standing collar and knotted cloth buttons
Became very fashionable in Shanghai in the 1920s and 1930s
A famous traditional dress from China

facts_and_myths.claim: A qipao has a high standing collar called a mandarin collar.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The short upright collar wraps neatly around the neck and is a key feature of the dress.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its knotted cloth fasteners are called frog buttons.

facts_and_myths.claim: The qipao and the cheongsam are two completely different dresses.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are the same dress; cheongsam is simply the Cantonese name for it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The qipao became a fashion hit in 1920s Shanghai.

name: Vietnamese Conical Hat
visual_anchor: A smiling farmer wearing a pale straw-colored cone-shaped hat with a ribbon chin strap, standing in a bright green rice paddy under a sunny sky, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A hat shaped like a pointy cone
Protects from both hot sun and pouring rain
Woven from palm leaves over thin bamboo rings
An iconic symbol of Vietnam, often worn with an ao dai

facts_and_myths.claim: This hat is woven from palm leaves stretched over bamboo rings.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Thin bamboo rings make the cone frame, and layers of dried palm leaves are stitched on top.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Special hats from Hue hide poems or pictures that appear when held up to sunlight.

facts_and_myths.claim: Conical hats are worn only in Vietnam.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Similar cone-shaped hats are worn across Asia, including in China, Cambodia and the Philippines.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The steep cone shape lets rain run off quickly, like a tiny roof.

name: Mooncake
visual_anchor: A round golden-brown pastry with a pretty flower pattern pressed on top, one cut open to show sweet filling and a bright yellow yolk center, on a plate under a full moon, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A small, rich pastry usually shaped like a circle
Its top has a pretty pattern pressed in by a mold
Often filled with sweet lotus seed or red bean paste
The star treat of the Mid-Autumn Festival

facts_and_myths.claim: Some mooncakes hide a salted egg yolk that looks like a full moon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A round, golden salted egg yolk sits in the middle of the sweet filling.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The patterns on top are pressed in using carved wooden or plastic molds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mooncakes are always round.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most are round like the full moon, but square mooncakes are common too, especially in Vietnam.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Snow skin mooncakes are a no-bake kind with a soft, chewy outer layer.

name: Banh Chung
visual_anchor: A neat square cake wrapped in bright green leaves and tied with thin bamboo strings, one slice cut to show green-tinted sticky rice and yellow bean filling, on a wooden table, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A square, savory cake wrapped in green leaves
Made from sticky rice, mung beans and pork
Boiled for many hours, often through the night
A must-have food for Vietnamese New Year

facts_and_myths.claim: Banh chung is boiled for many hours, often through the whole night.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Families take turns watching the pot while the thick rice cake cooks slowly all the way through.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A legend says its square shape stands for the Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Banh chung is a sweet dessert like a sponge cake.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It is savory, filled with mung beans and pork inside sticky rice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The leaves wrapped around it turn the outside of the rice green.

name: Red Envelope
visual_anchor: A grandmother smiling as she hands a shiny red envelope with golden flower patterns to a happy child in festive clothes, warm red decorations behind them, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A small, bright red paper gift
Usually decorated with shiny gold patterns
Elders give them to children with money tucked inside
A favorite tradition of Lunar New Year and Tet

facts_and_myths.claim: Red envelopes with money are given to children at Lunar New Year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Parents, grandparents and relatives give them to wish kids luck and good health in the new year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Red is chosen because it stands for good luck and happiness.

facts_and_myths.claim: Red envelopes are given only in China.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Families in Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia and many other places share red envelopes too.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many people use crisp, brand-new banknotes to make the gift feel fresh.

name: Paper Lantern
visual_anchor: Rows of round red, yellow and orange glowing lanterns with golden tassels hanging over a cozy evening street, warm soft light everywhere, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A glowing decoration that hangs up high
Made of thin paper stretched over a light frame
Round red ones often have golden tassels at the bottom
A classic sight at Lunar New Year and the Mid-Autumn Festival

facts_and_myths.claim: Paper lanterns are made of thin paper stretched over bamboo or wire.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The light frame gives the lantern its shape, and the thin paper lets the light glow through.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The old town of Hoi An in Vietnam glows with colorful lanterns on full-moon nights.

facts_and_myths.claim: Real candles are the safest way to light paper lanterns.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Paper can catch fire easily, so battery LED lights are much safer. Ask an adult to help.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lanterns can be shaped like stars, fish, rabbits and even dragons.

name: Lion Dance
visual_anchor: A bright red and gold lion costume with big blinking eyes and a fluffy mane leaping playfully in a festive street, drummers and cheering children nearby, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A lively street performance full of jumps and loud drums
Two dancers share one big, colorful costume
The creature blinks, shakes its head and nibbles lettuce
Performed for good luck at Lunar New Year and grand openings

facts_and_myths.claim: One lion costume is usually worked by two dancers, the head and tail.
facts_and_myths.explanation: One dancer moves the head and the other bends low as the back legs and tail.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The lion often 'eats' lettuce hung up high, then tosses the leaves out for good luck.

facts_and_myths.claim: The lion dance and the dragon dance are the same thing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A lion uses two dancers, while a long dragon is carried on poles by a whole team.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Drums, gongs and cymbals set the beat for every move the lion makes.

name: Jack-o'-Lantern
visual_anchor: A big orange pumpkin with a friendly carved smiling face glowing warmly from inside, sitting on a porch step beside autumn leaves and smaller pumpkins, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A round orange decoration that glows at night
A face is carved into it and a light is placed inside
Its insides are scooped out, seeds and all
The best-known decoration of Halloween

facts_and_myths.claim: Before pumpkins, people in Ireland carved faces into turnips.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Irish and Scottish families carved turnips and potatoes; pumpkins became popular later in America.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pumpkins are about 90 percent water.

facts_and_myths.claim: A jack-o'-lantern needs a real candle inside to glow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Battery LED lights glow just as nicely and are safer. Always ask an adult to do the carving.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The seeds scooped out of a pumpkin can be roasted into a crunchy snack.

name: Christmas Tree
visual_anchor: A tall green fir tree sparkling with colorful lights, shiny round ornaments and a golden star on top, wrapped gifts underneath in a cozy room, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A tall green tree brought indoors in winter
Decorated with lights, shiny balls and tinsel
Often topped with a star or an angel
Presents are placed underneath it for December 25

facts_and_myths.claim: London's Trafalgar Square gets a Christmas tree from Norway every year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Norway sends a giant tree each year as a thank-you gift to the people of Britain.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Norway has sent this tree every year since 1947.

facts_and_myths.claim: Christmas trees always had electric lights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early trees used small candles; electric string lights first appeared in the 1880s.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The first tinsel was made from very thin strips of real silver.

name: Gingerbread House
visual_anchor: A cute little brown cookie house with white icing snow on the roof, colorful gumdrops, candy canes and peppermint candies on the walls, on a snowy table, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A tiny house you can actually nibble
Its walls and roof are made of spiced cookies
White icing works as glue and as pretend snow
Built and decorated with candy at Christmastime

facts_and_myths.claim: Icing works like glue to hold gingerbread house walls together.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Thick royal icing dries hard, so it sticks the cookie walls and roof firmly in place.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gingerbread houses became popular in Germany around the time 'Hansel and Gretel' was published.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gingerbread houses are only for looking at and can't be eaten.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are made of real cookies and candy, so they are edible, though they get hard over time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bergen, Norway builds a whole miniature gingerbread town every holiday season.

name: Pinata
visual_anchor: A bright star-shaped paper party decoration with colorful tissue-paper points and streamers hanging from a tree at a sunny backyard party, excited kids gathered safely to the side, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A colorful party decoration hung up high
It is filled with candy and small toys
Kids take turns swinging a stick to break it open
A favorite tradition at Mexican celebrations and birthday parties

facts_and_myths.claim: Pinatas are filled with candy and small toys.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When it breaks open, the treats spill out. Everyone else should stand well back while someone swings.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name comes from the Italian word pignatta, meaning clay pot.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pinatas are always shaped like donkeys.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pinatas come in many shapes, and the classic Mexican pinata is a star with seven points.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditional pinatas were made from clay pots covered in colorful paper.

name: Rangoli
visual_anchor: A big round flower-shaped floor design made of bright pink, orange, yellow and blue powder and marigold petals at a doorway, tiny clay lamps glowing around it, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Colorful art made right on the floor
Created with colored powder, rice flour or flower petals
Often drawn at the doorway to welcome guests
A beloved Diwali decoration from India

facts_and_myths.claim: Rangoli patterns are made on the floor with colored powder or rice flour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Artists sprinkle powder, rice flour or petals by hand to form bright patterns on the ground.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In South India, a similar rice flour floor design is called kolam.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rangoli designs are made to last for years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rangoli is temporary art, swept away after the celebration and made fresh again next time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many rangoli designs are symmetrical, with matching sides like a snowflake.

name: Fireworks
visual_anchor: A family wrapped in blankets watching from a faraway grassy hill as giant red, gold and blue sparkling bursts light up the night sky over a city river, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Bright bursts of color that light up the night sky
They make loud booms, crackles and whistles
Big shows mark New Year's Eve and national holidays
First made in ancient China

facts_and_myths.claim: Different metals give fireworks their colors, like copper for blue.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tiny bits of metal make each color: strontium glows red, barium green and copper blue.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blue is one of the hardest firework colors to make bright.

facts_and_myths.claim: It is fine for kids to light fireworks by themselves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fireworks are only safe in trained adults' hands. Kids should watch from a safe distance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fireworks were first made in ancient China more than a thousand years ago.

name: Water Puppetry
visual_anchor: Shiny painted wooden puppets of smiling farmers, ducks and a golden dragon gliding across a pond stage in front of a red and gold pagoda-style screen, ripples sparkling, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A puppet show where the stage is a pool of water
Painted wooden puppets glide, splash and dance on the surface
Puppeteers hide behind a screen, standing in water
A folk art from the rice fields of northern Vietnam

facts_and_myths.claim: Water puppeteers hide behind a screen while standing in waist-deep water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They stay hidden behind a bamboo screen and move the puppets from underwater.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This art began in the flooded rice fields of northern Vietnam about a thousand years ago.

facts_and_myths.claim: Water puppets float freely and move all on their own.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Puppeteers control them with long poles and strings hidden under the water.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The puppets are carved from light fig wood and coated with shiny waterproof lacquer.
